title: How long till human AI game dev is made redundant, and no human input is required?
author: dntbeefontheinternet
selftext:
So the obvious conclusion of this technology is that all gamers will just have a personal gaming AI assistant, which will generate any game requested on the fly. 

User just suggests a genre or whatever - or as detailed as they would like - and could even modify rules and variables mid game, interact with the AI dev during play.

Individual AI assistants could hook up to collaborate for massive multi player.

The tasks that humans currently do in AI game dev is finite and shrinking.  How long till the whole lot is done by AI, and the gamers themselves are the only ones left with human input?

replies.author: CheekyChewingum
replies.body:
People don't know what they want. Also, novelty and unknown are a big part of entertainment.

Designing is the art of creating something that people will like (among other goals).

Stories are the easiest creative example. I can easily tell that I like a story or not but that doesn't mean I can write a good story.

I can type, I can speak but I can't design a good story. Mechanical skills are not enough. I can also not tell someone else what kind of story I will like before listening to it.

If I ask AI to write a good story, I mostly get disappointed.

comments.author: 0bscuris
comments.body:
People are very bad at recognizing and describing what they like. To qoute george carlin, think of how stupid the average person is and then realize half the people are dumber than that. 

I don’t think that we will ever get to point ur describing. I think there will be a subset of power users who do what ur talking about but most people will just buy something and play it and go on a thumbs up, thumbs down level of analysis.

That said, mods or iterative game design will be really fascinating. Right now cuz the technology is new, people r making games from scratch and distributing them via same system. 

U make game, i pay you, i play game. 

What is potentially possible is: instead of putting a game on steam you put it on git. A hundred people download it, they all make changes they think are good, they upload their branch, one branch becomes more popular, that branch continues the other die. 

Who made that game?

replies.author: Own_Principle_7901
replies.body:
> instead of putting a game on steam you put it on git. A hundred people download it, they all make changes they think are good, they upload their branch, one branch becomes more popular, that branch continues the other die.

Altough the idea is interesting, most games have a pretty short lifetime in a player's hand. Drastic majority of players won't ever touch the game again after they finish it. And most game are not replayable in their nature. 

If I played and beaten a game that was mostly solid, only having some balancing problems with certain itens I didn't felt like using, I won't be replaying the game if someone managed to fix these itens.

So the question is... Who will be playing all the branches to have a curated option of every single one of them to say which branch should die and who should be forked even further?

The number of people that make and play mods is small, but it doesn’t matter cuz they are hardcore.

replies.author: teapot_RGB_color
replies.body:
Because AI is, by design, to return the most common nominator based on the query. Or to put it in English, the most average.

This is by design, and the intended behaviour.

So the reason for you asking the question in such a way, means that you either have too little knowledge of entertainment or too little understanding of how AI works.

Now, you can ask if there is a market for a one-click game, and yes of course there is. There is a market for AI tik tok dramas already.

But it's equivalent of saying that it makes all other forms of video content redundant, which is not the case. Just like Candy Crush, with its endless clones, didn't compete with Demon's Souls on the gaming market.

replies.author: dntbeefontheinternet
replies.body:
No - I'm pretty sure that's not  really true. Maybe I don't understand AI as much as you, but I certainly know it's a lot more nuanced and deep than "the most average answer".

It entirely depends on how the model is trained and rewarded.  It gives the answer it probabilistically feels the user has demanded.

I can imagine an AI model and agent platform trained specifically to be an AI assistant  (and then ongoing training/feedback by the subscribed individual gamer) could in the near future generate pretty compelling results for the average gamer.

replies.author: teapot_RGB_color
replies.body:
Yes, you have it pretty correct.

It will search for the most obvious return based on the user input with a randomness to deviate from the path (temperature), more or less.

So, yes you'll be able to create a cookie cutter game pretty much polished, in the future, I think so.

And then you can further define exactly your preferences to tailor the result.

Well the challenge is about defining those preferences to a degree where it both provide a unique and interesting experience.

Because no one stupid enough, other then game developers, to sit down and think about specifically how much blinking rate the QT interaction icons should have.

Because all of these small decisions is what makes a game feel unique, and when they play together it feels even better.

All the grandiose stuff, like "I want a cizy fishing game in cyberpunk city" is not the uniqueness or what makes a game stand out or good, it's all the tiny decisions coming together.

So if you skip out on all those decisions, and LLM or genAI will naturally revert back to what is default and generic. And sometimes you want generic design, sometimes you don't, that's also part of that small decision set for every single thing.

depends on what game, copying someone's slop into another slop, or an actual game that people potentially remember. How will it know what to do without input? where is the creative aspect? design decisions? world building? I mean even games that are arcadey and more gameplay focused like ball x pit have a sense of world building, narrative, and uniqueness to them. The creative part is 90% of a game, if anything AI demonstrated how crucial (skilled) human input is.  
  
That's like telling AI "write a book. Include elves, a forest, and its genre is romance" and it'll write you 500 page novel that reads like something of a 2/10 netflix show,- perhaps enjoyable by those with low standards, immediately discarded by others.  
  
I feel like some people's gaming library consists of mobile apps, and that's alright for them, but that's like coming into a 5-star restaurant, sitting down, taking out a bag of potato chips and loudly commenting "when will we stop needing chefs" much to the confusion of others who know why they are there and the scope of what they can experience.
